title: New Minimally Invasive Treatment Promises Knee Pain Relief and Surgery Avoidance
subtitle: Genicular artery embolization emerges as an alternative for osteoarthritis sufferers seeking a middle‑ground solution.
excerpt: A minimally invasive procedure called genicular artery embolization (GAE) can markedly reduce knee osteoarthritis pain, offering a way to avoid joint replacement surgery.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
An emerging treatment may provide a fresh outlook for individuals looking to ease knee osteoarthritis pain while avoiding joint‑replacement surgery. The approach, known as genicular artery embolization (GAE), is a minimally invasive procedure positioned as a middle ground between conservative therapies and total knee replacement.

Genicular artery embolization works by targeting tiny blood vessels. The procedure blocks these small vessels that are linked to inflammation within the knee joint. By interrupting the inflammatory pathway—one of the main drivers of pain and discomfort in osteoarthritis patients—this technique aims to relieve symptoms.

Studies indicate that GAE can significantly cut pain levels. Patients have reported little to no pain after the procedure, highlighting its potential to improve quality of life. This notable pain reduction offers an option for those who need more relief than conservative measures provide but are not yet ready for—or wish to postpone—knee replacement surgery.

The durability of GAE’s benefits is also noteworthy. Research suggests that, in responders, positive effects can last from two to four years, granting a substantial relief window and allowing patients to manage the condition more effectively without immediate recourse to more invasive interventions.

Knee osteoarthritis affects joint cartilage, leading to pain, swelling, and limited mobility. Conservative treatments typically include physical therapy, analgesic medications, and injections. In contrast, knee replacement is a major surgery that removes damaged cartilage and bone, substituting them with artificial components. By presenting itself as a “middle‑ground,” genicular artery embolization fills a gap, offering a less invasive alternative to major surgery while delivering pain relief that surpasses early‑stage conservative therapies.

With information from ScienceDaily.
